Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette: Maria, a 40-year-old European woman and data scientist, witnessed a traumatic event during her recent trip to Israel. She had been visiting an Arab village when she saw a small fire break out in one of the buildings, which quickly spread due to dry conditions. Despite her attempts to evacuate those inside, several people were injured, including children, leaving Maria deeply shaken. Since returning home, Maria has found herself constantly triggered by reminders of that fateful day. The sight of Arab villages on television or even passing images of flames in advertisements bring back the intense fear and helplessness she experienced. Her triggers are so potent because they instantly transport her back to the chaos and urgency of that moment, making it feel as if the event is happening all over again. Maria has been throwing herself into work to keep her mind occupied, working long hours to avoid being alone with her thoughts. This has become a maladaptive strategy for dealing with the stress and trauma she carries inside. She often finds herself rumination on why this happened to her and what could have been done differently to prevent it. The more she works, the less time she spends engaging in normal activities or spending quality time with her husband. Maria’s flashbacks are frequent and vivid, feeling just as real and immediate as they did during the actual event. She hears the sounds of screaming and sizzling flames in her head at unexpected moments, which often leave her feeling on edge and hypervigilant. This hyperarousal has led to a heightened sense of threat from strangers approaching her even in ordinary situations, like walking down the street or waiting for an elevator. Her fear is compounded by a persistent belief that she should have done more to protect others and failed. She often compares herself to how someone else might have handled the situation differently, leading to intense feelings of self-blame and inadequacy. These negative appraisals are deeply rooted in her experience and contribute to her growing sense that her life may not be worth living anymore. Maria’s attempts at managing these symptoms include repeatedly checking doors and windows for security. She finds herself constantly reassessing the safety of her environment, which only exacerbates her anxiety. Her overworking has strained her relationship with her husband, who feels neglected as she spends most of her time buried in work to avoid dealing with her trauma. Despite her efforts to maintain control through excessive working and avoidance behaviors, Maria’s symptoms have continued to worsen. The persistent memories and flashbacks have made it increasingly difficult for her to function at work and home. She has become more isolated, pushing away support from friends and family who offer to help but don't understand the depth of her distress. What finally brought Maria to seek help was a moment where she found herself unable to sleep due to intrusive memories and auditory recall of that day in Israel. Her husband had noticed a significant change in her behavior and urged her to see someone. Deep down, Maria is most afraid of being overwhelmed by the traumatic memories and losing control completely. She hopes for a way to regain some normalcy in her life and to find a sense of peace with what happened. In her current state, Maria seeks understanding and relief from the constant barrage of triggers and negative thoughts. She is hopeful that therapy can provide her with tools to cope more effectively and eventually come to terms with her experience.
